newsitem.title: UK: Sickly gold weaker but off lows in London.
newsitem.headline: Sickly gold weaker but off lows in London.

text.p: Gold prices edged up from early lows on Thursday, although dealers thought it likely that they would soon renew the slide that has taken them down 3-1/2 percent since the start of the year.
"It looks like gold could consolidate today before the funds and speculators smack it down to $350, which is what they appear to have in mind," a London-based dealer said.
"Below that, who knows what the objective is."
Bullion was fixed at $354.50 an ounce, down sharply from Wednesday's afternoon fixing of $356.60. It has tumbled nearly $15 since the start of year when market weakness intensified.
Prices took a hit overnight in fund-driven selling out of New York and then Australian producer selling in Asia, dipping to below $354 an ounce at one point, dealers said.
"If producers are selling, they expect prices to decline further and want to lock in higher prices," an analyst said. "They're going to be selling into any small rally."
But physical offtake, mostly from the Middle East, was helping buoy prices in European trading, he added.
However, analysts said they saw little to support gold above $350 an ounce, which has not been seen since early October 1993.
News that Russian President Boris Yeltsin was in hospital with pneumonia had no effect on the market, despite gold's traditional role as a store of value in times of political and economic turmoil.

"No one cared when he had open-heart surgery (in November). Why should they care if he has pneumonia?" a trader said. Silver and platinum were little changed from Wednesday's closing levels, but were vulnerable to losses with gold.
Silver was one cent higher at $4.66/$4.68, while platinum was off by $0.50 at $358.50/$359.50.
Palladium, in sharp contrast to the other downtrending precious metals, fixed at a near four-month high of $121.85 an ounce, up $1.85 from the previous fixing.
"Prices are rising on consumer and speculative demand, amid Russian supply concerns," a London-based dealer noted.

Supply contract talks between Japanese trade houses and Russia's platinum group exporting agency have been delayed, prompting Japanese traders to cover their needs in the spot market, dealers said. Japan is the world's largest consumer of platinum group metals, including palladium, while Russia is the largest producer of palladium.
